meeting is being audio recorded. It is not being video recorded, and it is not being live streamed. But it is being audio recorded. to our information items, starting with item 4.01, the audit universe. And I will turn it over to you, Mr. Woods. Well, thank you, and good afternoon and welcome back, Chair Donahue. It's good to see you. All right. Well, today I am presenting the Office of the Auditor General's Fiscal Year 2027 audit universe. This presentation outlines how we identified risk across the division and how we are prioritizing our audit resources for the upcoming

fiscal year. Next slide, please. First off, what is the audit universe? I want to briefly explain what the audit universe represents. The audit universe is our comprehensive inventory of areas across the organization that could be audited. It serves as a risk map, giving transparency into where the most significant risks exist. For fiscal year 2027, we identified 38 auditable

topics across nine risk areas. However, due to our staffing, three auditors, two staff, and myself, we realistically have the capacity to complete four to six audits per year. So importantly, this is not a commitment to audit everything on the list. It's a view of risk across the division. In terms of how this was developed, we used a structured risk assessment

approach that included principal and senior staff surveys, input from school board, public discussions, including audit committees, LA and P committees, and school board meetings, external K-12 context, and professional judgment based on audit experience. This gives us a balanced and well-informed view of the risks here in the division.

Highest-risk topics. From that universe, we identified the highest-risk areas based on potential financial, legal, and operational impact. At the critical risk level, a few key areas stand out. Federal grant compliance, where non-compliance could result in repayment of funds, especially in ESSER closeout. Oracle ERMP implementation, which touches payroll,

procurement, and financial reporting simultaneously. Cybersecurity preparedness. Given the high level of ransomware activity in K-12, that is always going to be a high risk that we face here in the division and across the nation. Procurement controls, where risks lie like purchase order splitting are just known fraud vectors, and so it's more of a function of purchase orders as opposed to it being a

function of weak controls here. That is not why that is a critical risk level. It is just the nature of it dealing with high numbers of dollars. Mr. Woods, sorry. Okay, so I don't know exactly off the top of my head anymore what the ESSER

Thank you. And my other potentially stupid question, you've divided here on this slide categories of critical risk and high risk.

Thank you ... the next upcoming slides. But critical risk would pose a higher risk to the school division than high risk. So, that is correct. And so there are several high risks, as we just mentioned, and those include employer reporting and retaliation oversight, compensation

equity, vendor contract oversight. These areas collectively represent where breakdowns would have the most significant impact on the division. Next slide, please. Risk ratings and prioritization. While risk ratings are important, they are not the only factor in determining what we audit. Two additional considerations drive prioritization. First is likelihood.

Some high-impact risks may already have a strong control or recent audit coverage, which lowers the urgency for immediate review, which addresses your prior question, Chair Donahue, that if it's a critical risk, does it mean it is high on our list of necessary audits. Second is competing priorities and capacity restraints. With a team of three

staff members and a maximum of four to six audits per year, we have to make deliberate choices even among high-risk areas. Our goal is to deploy resources where we can add the most value, not simply perform the most highest or critical risk areas. Another important lens is audit complexity. This reflects how difficult an audit is to execute,

not how important it is. We group topics into low complexity, clear standards, and easy-to-verify evidence. Moderate complexity, multiple stakeholders, and structured processes. High complexity, sensitive areas or those lacking clear standards. One key point here, a topic does not need to be complex to be important. For example, a lower complexity audit can still address a critical risk.
This helps us balance our audit plan between impact and feasibility. And I'll just give you a moment there if you want to review the audits across the spectrum.

All right. We'll head to the next slide. You'll notice that some topics remain in the audit universe, but are not endorsed for the fiscal year 2027 annual audit plan. Workforce capacity, which requires more trend data.

Capital projects, which is high risk, but may be beyond our current capacity of three staff members. And I mention that because, as a school division, we are obligated to perform school activity fund audits annually, and that is performed by Business and Financial Services, which allows us to audit other areas within the division that are not covered within that area. on risk, likelihood, complexity, available resources, and impact. So there's a likelihood that an event can occur, and what is the impact it would have on the division if that event were to occur? rates, the rates would be based on those negotiated rates. For anybody who doesn't fall under the CBA, then we would perform an analysis. I will cover five areas, objective and scope of the engagement, overall design, assessment and maturity, key strengths Priority design gaps and associated risks, and a summary of

our overall perspective and governance takeaways. The goal here is to provide a structured view of how the framework is functioning today and where it can be strengthened. Next slide. individual performance. The overall framework is generally effective with some targeted design enhancements. We assessed it at level III, defined maturity on a scale of one to five. For example, emerging risks,

sensitive issues, and non-routine events. So the takeaway here is the foundation is sound, but resilience under more complex conditions can be strengthened. Next slide. To highlight key strengths, there are several areas where the framework is working as intended. First, governance design.

accurate, reliable, and decision-supportive. So overall, the core structure is functioning well and aligned with expected governance practices here in LCPS. Next slide, please.
